title: Performance analysis in football: A critical review and implications for future research
author_source: Rob Mackenzie, Christopher J. Cushion, Journal of Sports Sciences 31(6), 639-676, online 2012, article
note: Most-cited critical review of football performance analysis: argues the field overemphasises predictive variables, questions sample sizes and variable definitions, and calls for research on athlete and coach learning. Sets up the central tension between counting events and changing behaviour.
course_use: Core reading; check WU licence

title: Match Analysis in Team Ball Sports: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
author_source: Hugo Sarmento, Filipe Manuel Clemente, José Roberto Afonso et al., Sports Medicine - Open 8(1), 66, 2022, article
note: Umbrella review of 24 systematic reviews across team ball sports; AMSTAR-2 rates confidence critically low in 12 of them. Maps four levels of analysis from dyad to team and shows neglected areas (psychosocial, women's game, match context). Fast route to the state of the evidence.
course_use: Background reading; open access

title: Why Does Soccer Performance Research Disagree? A Critical Review of Contradictory Findings and Methodological Challenges
author_source: Spyridon Plakias, Studia sportiva 20(2), 2026, article
note: Case-based narrative review explaining why studies on running performance and ball possession contradict each other: ignored context, inconsistent definitions, lost tactical meaning, weak statistics. Short and well suited to a seminar on reading match-analysis research critically.
course_use: Seminar reading; open access

title: Reliability procedures for categorical data in Performance Analysis
author_source: Nic James, Joe Taylor, Simon Stanley, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 7(1), 1-11, 2007, article
note: Standard methods paper for reliability of categorical coding: gold-standard comparison and Yule's Q with a 0.95 threshold. Older, but still the reference when students test their own tagging templates.
course_use: Lab reading for a coding reliability exercise; check WU licence

title: Inter-operator reliability of live football match statistics from OPTA Sportsdata
author_source: Hongyou Liu, Will G. Hopkins, A. Miguel Gómez et al., International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 13(3), 803-821, 2013, article
note: Inter-operator reliability of Opta live data from one Spanish league match: kappa 0.92 and 0.94 for team events, mean event time difference 0.06 s. Caveat: single match, trained operators, one vendor's system. Good basis for discussing what 'reliable' means for commercial data.
course_use: Reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: Analysing the reliability of technical and tactical data used in football performance analysis
author_source: Jong-Won Kim, Chung-Hyeon Na, Korean Journal of Sports Science 33(3), 713-730, 2024, article
note: Review of 164 football articles from 1990 to 2023: 75.6% ran reliability tests, 57.3% named the test, 55.5% reported values; kappa dominates. Useful evidence that reliability reporting remains patchy. Lower-tier journal, so use for the numbers rather than the argument.
course_use: Background; check WU licence

title: Event detection in football: Improving the reliability of match analysis
author_source: Jonas Bischofberger, Arnold Baca, Erich Schikuta, PLoS ONE 19(4), e0298107, 2024, article
note: Vienna-based validation of rule-based pass and shot detection on four datasets. F-scores reach 0.92 for passes only when event and position data are dependent, and fall to 0.71 (passes) and 0.65 (shots) when independent: published accuracy is likely overstated. Excellent on validation design.
course_use: Core reading for data validity; open access

title: VERSA: Verified Event Data Format for Reliable Soccer Analytics
author_source: Geonhee Jo, Mingu Kang, Kangmin Lee et al., arXiv preprint, 2026, preprint
note: Verification framework for event streams: finds logical inconsistencies in 18.81% of K League 1 2024 events from one provider and shows downstream effects on VAEP. Preprint, one league, but gives a concrete, teachable picture of event-data errors.
course_use: Lab or seminar reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: The Role of Video Technology in Football Coaching: An Integrative Review
author_source: Antti Nyman, Antti Ekonoja, Tommi Kärkkäinen et al., International Sport Coaching Journal 13(2), 359-371, online 2025, article
note: Integrative review of 34 articles on video technology in football coaching, with a framework linking technological, coaching and football knowledge. Names opportunities (team play, player involvement) and limits (overreliance, mental workload, manual video work). Best current entry point to the topic.
course_use: Core reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: Analysing coach–athlete ‘talk in interaction’ within the delivery of video-based performance feedback in elite youth soccer
author_source: Ryan Groom, Christopher J. Cushion, Lee Nelson, Qualitative Research in Sport Exercise and Health 4(3), 439-458, 2012, article
note: Conversation analysis of six Premier League Academy video sessions over a season: the coach controls turn-taking, topics and questioning. Classic demonstration that a video session is a social and power event. Could be paired with students transcribing a mock session.
course_use: Reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: A coach’s political use of video-based feedback: a case study in elite-level academy soccer
author_source: Michael Booroff, Lee Nelson, Paul Potrac, Journal of Sports Sciences 34(2), 116-124, 2015, article
note: Case study of an academy head coach (6 interviews, 10 observations) using video to meet club expectations, a micropolitical reading of analysis technology. Useful counterweight to the view of video as neutral information.
course_use: Seminar reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: No Place to Hide: Football Players' and Coaches' Perceptions of the Psychological Factors Influencing Video Feedback
author_source: Simon Middlemas, Chris Harwood, Journal of Applied Sport Psychology 30(1), 23-44, 2017, article
note: Interviews with 11 coaches and 12 players in elite youth football on psychological responses, delivery strategies and climate of video feedback. Practical for designing feedback sessions and for discussing player exposure.
course_use: Reading; free repository or preprint copy available

title: Objectivity of match analysis in football: Testing the level of agreement between coaches’ interpretations of video data
author_source: Philip Furley, Saumya Mehta, Dominik Raabe et al., International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching 20(1), 45-55, online 2024, article
note: Three studies (N = 15, 24, 16) where coaches view the same footage and disagree even on team formation; Fleiss kappa from -.036 to .236. Striking and easily replicated in class. Small samples and simple questions are the caveat.
course_use: Core reading; in-class replication; check WU licence

title: Examining how data becomes information for an upcoming opponent in football
author_source: Saumya Mehta, Philip Furley, Dominik Raabe et al., International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching 19(3), 978-987, online 2023, article
note: 12 analysts build opponent reports from identical video, event and position data; annotated video dominates, and professional coaches barely agree on report quality (ICC 0.147). Directly relevant to the analyst-to-coach handover and to an opposition-report assignment.
course_use: Core reading; assignment model; check WU licence

title: Applied performance analysts in association football: A scoping review of roles, challenges, and opportunities (2010–2025)
author_source: Thomas Anthony Mitchell, Don Vinson, John Francis, International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching, 2026, article
note: PRISMA-ScR scoping review, 36 papers from 2010 to 2025, on applied analysts in football. Two themes, ambiguity and stakeholders; roles move from data collection to data translation amid unclear accreditation. Best single overview of the profession.
course_use: Core reading; open access

title: ‘I code as much as I can because you never know what they might ask for’. The role of the coach in Performance Analysis: The view of the analyst
author_source: Claire Mulvenna, Daniel Bloyce, Craig Twist et al., International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching 19(6), 2345-2355, 2024, article
note: Reflexive thematic analysis of interviews with eight full-time analysts in English league and non-league football; themes include 'flying solo', 'the reticent coach' and 'autocratic presentations'. Shows how much coding is defensive. Good voice-of-practice text.
course_use: Reading; open access

title: The importance of appearing trustworthy in the workplace: performance analysts’ perspectives
author_source: Lee Nelson, Nic James, Scott Nicholls et al., Sport Education and Society 30(2), 249-265, online 2023, article
note: Survey of 88 analysts on appearing trustworthy, including concealing known information from athletes alongside coaching staff. Raises a discussable ethics point about analyst practice. Self-report, across sports rather than football only.
course_use: Seminar reading; open access

title: Developing a framework for professional practice in applied performance analysis
author_source: Denise Martin, Peter G. O Donoghue, Jonathan Bradley et al., International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 21(6), 845-888, 2021, article
note: Framework for applied performance analysis from a systematic review of 90 papers, validated with 24 experts: nine components of practice (from needs analysis to service review) and five areas of expertise. Usable as the structure of the applied workflow.
course_use: Reading; framework for project work; free repository or preprint copy available

title: The role of the analyst: comparative analysis of applied performance analyst job advertisements in the UK and Ireland (2021-2022)
author_source: John William Francis, Jamie Lee Kyte, Michael Bateman, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport 24(4), 331-360, 2024, article
note: Content analysis of 130 UK and Irish analyst job adverts from 2021 to 2022 across 21 role titles: technical expertise is prioritised over relationship skills. Good for career discussion and skills mapping. All sports, not only football.
course_use: Reading; careers exercise; open access

title: Data analytics practices and reporting strategies in senior football: insights into athlete health and performance from over 200 practitioners worldwide
author_source: Antonio Dello Iacono, Naomi Datson, Jo Clubb et al., Science and Medicine in Football 10(1), 80-95, online 2025, article
note: Survey of 206 practitioners across all six FIFA confederations on who collects what and how; exploratory analysis 90%, predictive modelling the least common, spreadsheets still popular. Reality check against vendor narratives.
course_use: Background; open access

title: Validation of electronic performance and tracking systems EPTS under field conditions
author_source: Daniel Linke, Daniel Link, Martin Lames, PLoS ONE 13(7), e0199519, 2018, article
note: Compares video, radar LPS and GPS against VICON in 14 U19 players: position error 56 cm (video), 23 cm (LPS), 96 cm (GPS), and over 40% deviation for high-speed distance on every system. The standard reference that systems are not comparable. Hardware has since moved on.
course_use: Core reading on tracking validity; open access

title: Football-specific validity of TRACAB’s optical video tracking systems
author_source: Daniel Linke, Daniel Link, Martin Lames, PLoS ONE 15(3), e0230179, 2020, article
note: TRACAB Gen4 and Gen5 against VICON in 20 players: position RMSE 0.08 to 0.09 m. Frames with obviously failed tracking were excluded, which is the caveat to teach. Read with the 2018 Linke paper to show progress and limits.
course_use: Reading; open access

title: Interchangeability of optical tracking technologies: potential overestimation of the sprint running load demands in the English Premier League
author_source: Matt Taberner, Tom Allen, Jason O’keefe et al., Science and Medicine in Football 7(4), 374-383, 2022, article
note: Three matches tracked at once by Prozone and TRACAB: total distance interchangeable, but mean bias in sprint distance of 61%. Shows why historical trends across tracking systems need care. Small match sample.
course_use: Reading; check WU licence

title: Concurrent validity of computer-vision artificial intelligence player tracking software using broadcast footage
author_source: Zachary L. Crang, Rich D. Johnston, Katie L. Mills et al., Journal of Sports Analytics 12, 2026, article
note: Three commercial AI trackers on broadcast footage from one 2022 World Cup match against TRACAB Gen 5: position RMSE 1.68 to 16.39 m, total distance bias from -21.8% to 24.3%. Tactical feed works best. Key evidence for what broadcast tracking can deliver; one match only.
course_use: Core reading; open access

title: Optical tracking in team sports
author_source: Pegah Rahimian, László Toka, Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports 18(1), 35-57, 2022, article
note: Survey of optical tracking written for quantitative analysts: taxonomy of conventional and deep learning methods, preprocessing, costs and limits. Bridges computer vision and sports analytics readers.
course_use: Technical background; free to read at publisher

title: Unlocking the potential of big data to support tactical performance analysis in professional soccer: A systematic review
author_source: Floris R. Goes, Laurentius A. Meerhoff, Murilo José de Oliveira Bueno et al., European Journal of Sport Science 21(4), 481-496, online 2020, article
note: Systematic review of 73 papers using position tracking data for tactical analysis, with a multidisciplinary framework for feature construction, modelling and interpretation. Clear on spatial and temporal aggregation problems.
course_use: Reading; open access

title: Attacking Key Performance Indicators in Soccer: Current Practice and Perceptions from the Elite to Youth Academy Level
author_source: Mat Herold, Matthias Kempe, Pascal Bauer et al., Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 20(1), 158-169, 2021, article
note: Survey of 145 practitioners in 42 countries: 83% use event data, 52% positional; preference for simple shot-related KPIs and low perceived value of newer metrics. Useful on the research-to-practice gap.
course_use: Reading; open access

title: Are Current Physical Match Performance Metrics in Elite Soccer Fit for Purpose or Is the Adoption of an Integrated Approach Needed?
author_source: Paul S. Bradley, J Ade, International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 13(5), 656-664, 2018, article
note: Commentary arguing that distance-by-speed metrics are one-dimensional and should be tied to tactical actions, the origin of the integrated physical-tactical approach. Conceptual; the authors note the evidence still needs building.
course_use: Reading; free to read at publisher

title: Perspectives on data analytics for gaining a competitive advantage in football: computational approaches to tactics
author_source: Sigrid B. H. Olthof, Jesse J. Davis, Science and Medicine in Football 10(2), 236-248, online 2025, article
note: Commentary linking computational football research with sports science: tactics evaluation, player and team prediction, movement modelling, automated match analysis. A compact map of a literature most sport scientists do not read.
course_use: Reading; open access

title: A Goal Scoring Probability Model for Shots Based on Synchronized Positional and Event Data in Football (Soccer)
author_source: Gabriel Anzer, Pascal Bauer, Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 3, 624475, 2021, article
note: xG model from 105,627 Bundesliga shots using synchronised positional and event data, validated statistically and with professional analysts. Good worked example of feature choice and calibration.
course_use: Lab reading; open access

title: Dealing With Randomness in Match Outcomes: How to Rethink Performance Evaluation in European Club Football Using Expected Goals
author_source: Marc Brechot, Raphael Flepp, Journal of Sports Economics 21(4), 335-362, 2020, article
note: Sports-economics paper using xG to separate performance from randomness, with a chart for spotting when results mislead club decision makers. Particularly fitting for a business school audience.
course_use: Core reading for management angle; check WU licence

title: A framework for the fine-grained evaluation of the instantaneous expected value of soccer possessions
author_source: Javier Fernández, Luke Bornn, Daniel Cervone, Machine Learning 110(6), 1389-1427, 2021, article
note: Expected possession value decomposed into pass, drive and shot components from tracking data, with interpretable probability surfaces. Reference model for possession value; demanding technically and needs proprietary data.
course_use: Advanced reading; open access

title: Actions Speak Louder than Goals
author_source: Tom Decroos, Lotte Bransen, Jan Van Haaren et al., ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD), 1851-1861, 2019, conference paper
note: Introduces SPADL and VAEP, valuing every on-ball action by its effect on scoring and conceding. Works on event data, so it can be reproduced in a student lab.

title: Space and Control in Soccer
author_source: Florian Martens, Uwe Dick, Ulf Brefeld, Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 3, 676179, 2021, article

title: An integrated dataset of spatiotemporal and event data in elite soccer
author_source: Manuel Bassek, Robert Rein, Hendrik Weber et al., Scientific Data 12(1), 195, 2025, article

title: SoccerNet-v2: A Dataset and Benchmarks for Holistic Understanding of Broadcast Soccer Videos
author_source: Adrien Deliège, Anthony Cioppa, Silvio Giancola et al., IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), 4503-4514, 2021, conference paper

title: SoccerNet Game State Reconstruction: End-to-End Athlete Tracking and Identification on a Minimap
author_source: Vladimir Somers, Victor Joos, Anthony Cioppa et al., IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Workshops (CVPRW), 3293-3305, 2024, conference paper

title: MSc Sport Performance Analysis
author_source: Leeds Beckett University, master's degree with PgCert and PgDip exit awards
note: Skill: preparation to work as a performance analyst. A course specification confirms PgCert and PgDip as contained awards. The page body did not load in the fetch tool, so fees, modules and current intake are unconfirmed.
course_use: Further UK degree option. Paid degree.

title: Introduction to Sport Performance Analysis (certificate)
author_source: Northumbria University, CPD short course by Angela Hibbs and Marc Briggs
note: Skill: what analysis is, how to interpret it, how to apply it to coaching and training. Distance learning with six months of access and tutor feedback, rolling start. Non-accredited, multi-sport; level: beginner. University-run at low cost.
course_use: Optional low-cost foundation. About GBP 225.

title: MSc in Soccer Analytics
author_source: Sports Data Campus with UCAM and MIU City University Miami, online master
note: Skill: providers, advanced metrics, Python and R, machine learning, Tableau and Power BI, thesis project in a club. Triple certification, on-site weekend in Miami and New York, 25 places in the first edition. Length and tuition not stated; heavy marketing language, so verify accreditation.
course_use: Career pointer on the analytics route. Paid, price on request.

title: Foundations of Sports Analytics: Data, Representation, and Models in Sports
author_source: University of Michigan on Coursera, Wenche Wang and Stefan Szymanski, MOOC
note: Skill: Python, regression and team performance with sports data, including an English Premier League lab. Six modules, about 5 weeks at 10 hours per week. Level: intermediate. Not video-based; first of five courses in the Sports Performance Analytics specialization. Open for enrolment.
course_use: Statistics refresher for the data block. Free audit option; certificate paid.

title: Certificate in Football Scouting
author_source: Barça Innovation Hub, online certificate
note: Skill: scouting with practical video analysis workflows on professional platforms; no dedicated video module in the syllabus. 4 months, next start 16 November 2026, certificate from Barça Innovation Hub. Older diplomas in tactical analysis were listed at about EUR 1200 but their pages have moved, so availability is unclear.
course_use: Career pointer. About EUR 675.

title: TSG Hoffenheim: Football in the Age of Analytics (A), with supplement (B)
author_source: Feng Zhu, Karim R. Lakhani, Sascha L. Schmidt, Kerry Herman, Harvard Business School, case 616-010, 2015 (rev. 2017); supplement 620-055, 2019; teaching note 620-067, 2019
note: The best true teaching case for this topic and it is German. Owner Dietmar Hopp (SAP co-founder) asks in 2015 whether technology and analytics, including the Footbonaut, justify their cost at a club not yet cash-flow positive, and whether a moneyball approach can work in football. 35 pages. The (B) supplement and joint teaching note were confirmed in HBS listings. Dated on tools: it is about training technology and strategy more than video analysis, so pair it with a current analyst account.
course_use: Case discussion on whether analytics pays. Paid, 11.95 USD per copy on the HBR store; educator copies via Harvard Business Publishing; check WU licence.

title: Brøndby IF Football Club: Leveraging Sports Analytics
author_source: Simon Ruder, Philippe Mogens Helmbæk, Emil Holmenlund Nymand, Xiao Xiao, Ning Su, Ivey Publishing, case W33343, 2023
note: Follows a mid-budget Danish club building analytics capabilities from 2015 to the end of 2022. 14 pages, written with Copenhagen Business School authors for graduate and undergraduate courses in sports analytics and digitalization. Learning goals cover what helps or hinders building data capabilities, which suits a business-school audience. The closest business case to a realistic club analyst department; it is about capability building rather than video tagging itself.
course_use: Case discussion on organising an analytics function. Paid, 10.54 USD listed on Ivey; teaching notes appear to need a free educator account; check WU licence.

title: Negotiating with Data: Analytics FC (A) and (B)
author_source: Jillian Jordan, Livia Alfonsi, Harvard Business School, cases 925-014 and 925-015, January 2025
note: A UK football consultancy uses data to support Alex Greenwood in her contract talks with Manchester City, its first female client. Part A (19 pp.) sets up the structural barriers in women's football, Part B (5 pp.) gives the analysis and outcome. Useful for how performance data is turned into an argument for a sceptical audience, and for women's football. It is a negotiation case, not a video analysis case.
course_use: Case discussion or role play on communicating data. Paid, 11.95 USD for (A) and 5.00 USD for (B) on the HBR store; check WU licence.

title: ReSpo.Vision: The Kickstart of an AI Sports Revolution
author_source: Paul A. Gompers, Elena Corsi, Nikolina Jonsson, Harvard Business School, case 824-151, February 2024
note: Growth of a Polish computer vision start-up that extracts player tracking data from ordinary single-camera footage. The only true HBS case found on a football tracking or computer vision firm. It is framed around entrepreneurship in an emerging ecosystem, so the technical content may be limited; the case text was not read, and the HBS page blocked automated fetching.
course_use: Case discussion on the market for tracking data and start-up strategy. Paid via Harvard Business Publishing, price not seen; check WU licence.

title: Data-driven Dominance: Empowering Indian Strikers with Sports Analytics in Football
author_source: Sharma et al., SAGE Business Cases, 2025
note: A struggling Indian club hires an AI analytics consultant to find where to improve its chance of winning; keywords include logistic regression, so it can double as a modelling exercise. The club appears fictionalised. Only the catalogue snippet was seen because the page redirects to a login.
course_use: Short quantitative case. SAGE Business Cases, institutional login; check WU licence.

title: Teaming Up the Right People: Selecting a Winning Football Team
author_source: Sanjeev et al., SAGE Business Cases, 2025
note: Decision-analysis case on player selection using a table of performance features and definitions. Good small exercise on how metric definitions drive selection, but it concerns player choice and not video analysis. Only the catalogue snippet was seen.
course_use: Short decision-analysis exercise. SAGE Business Cases, institutional login; check WU licence.

title: Build-your-own mini-case: Brentford and Midtjylland (no published teaching case found)
author_source: Guillermo Martinez-Arastey, Sport Performance Analysis, 2018, article; use with Sean Ingle, The Guardian, 2020
note: Searches of HBS, Ivey, SAGE and the web found no formal teaching case on Brentford, Midtjylland or Liverpool's data department. This secondary article supplies usable facts: the 2012 rescue by Matthew Benham, KPI-led recruitment, the 2015 dismissal of Mark Warburton after promotion over data-led scouting, and the closure of the academy. Several claims rest on third-party reporting, so students should test them.
course_use: Instructor-built mini-case on analytics against traditional judgement. Free web article.

title: DataCoach: a WU student start-up on affordable match analysis
author_source: WU Entrepreneurship and Innovation project course, Summer Semester 2020, project page
note: No WU teaching case on football analytics was found, but this WU student project works as local case material. The team interviewed more than 100 amateur clubs and found most analyse manually, have small budgets, and that about half already film their matches. Planned price was 160 euros per month. It is a short project summary and not a written case, with no teaching note. Compare with zone14 and Veo.
course_use: Discussion or start-up pricing exercise, WU-specific. Free web page; the team may be worth contacting.

title: Lab: Soccermatics event-data course with StatsBomb and Wyscout notebooks
author_source: David Sumpter, Uppsala University, online course materials, ongoing
note: Not a case but the most complete ready-made classroom lab: event data, xG, pass networks, expected threat, pitch control, clustering and a web app. The Uppsala version is a 5-credit course with hand-ins and expects statistics, linear algebra, calculus and programming, so a management cohort needs a reduced path through shot maps and xG.
course_use: Data lab in Python. Notes and code free online; the professional version listed at 1,600 euros is not needed.

title: Lab: Friends of Tracking code for Metrica tracking data and passing networks
author_source: Friends of Tracking Data, GitHub organisation, repositories last updated 2020 to 2023
note: Six small repositories, including LaurieOnTracking for Metrica tracking data and passing networks from event and tracking data. Good for showing students what tracking data looks like. Largely unmaintained since 2023 and no maintainers are named, so test the code before class.
course_use: Data lab in Python or R. Free, MIT licence on most repositories.

title: TacticAI: DeepMind and Liverpool FC on corner kicks
author_source: Zhe Wang, Petar Veličković and 21 others, Nature Communications, 2024, peer-reviewed article
note: AI assistant developed with Liverpool FC experts that predicts receivers and shots and suggests changed player setups for corners. Its suggestions were preferred over real setups 90% of the time in a blind expert study, and top retrievals were rated relevant 63% of the time against a 33% benchmark. The evaluation is qualitative and small, and uses only one club's experts; no evidence that corners actually improved in matches. DeepMind's blog (19 March 2024) is a readable companion.
course_use: Discussion of AI as analyst support and of what counts as validation. Open access.

title: FIFA Enhanced Football Intelligence: how the World Cup 2022 metrics were built
author_source: Chris Loxston, Juan Busso, Arron Ackermann, FIFA Training Centre, 2022, staff interview
note: FIFA's analysts explain merging live events with tracking data so that every event has all player positions, and how line breaks and the in-contest share are interpreted in context. A governing body describing its own product, so read alongside the independent test below.
course_use: Background and class discussion on new metrics. Free.

title: Are EFI data valuable? Independent test on the 2022 World Cup group stage
author_source: Biology of Sport, online 2023, peer-reviewed article
note: Independent check of FIFA's metrics: goals correlated with completed defensive line breaks and receptions behind the defensive line, and attempts on target with receptions, final third entries and line breaks. Group stage only and correlational. Useful for teaching students to test a vendor or federation metric against outcomes.
course_use: Reading plus short replication discussion. Open access.

title: Semi-automated offside technology at the 2022 World Cup
author_source: FIFA, 2022, media release
note: Primary announcement of the 12-camera system with a connected ball, with referees staying responsible for decisions. Useful for the human-in-the-loop point. FIFA says that for 2026 clear offsides go directly to on-field officials, which was seen only in a search snippet; the newer FIFA page returned 404 when fetched.
course_use: Background example of computer vision in officiating. Free.

title: VAR raised decision accuracy from 92.1% to 98.3%
author_source: Spitz, Wagemans and others, Journal of Sports Sciences, 2020, peer-reviewed article
note: 2,195 matches in 13 countries, 9,732 checks and 795 reviews, with a median on-field review of 62 seconds. Rare large field evidence on video review. The ground truth comes from within the officiating system, a limit students should question.
course_use: Reading and critique of measurement. Paid journal; check WU licence.

title: Premier League Key Match Incidents panel on VAR errors
author_source: ESPN, February 2025, news report on Premier League figures
note: After 23 rounds in 2024-25 the five-member panel counted 13 VAR errors (4 incorrect interventions, 9 missed), against 20 and 29 in the two prior seasons. Good for discussing who audits a video system. The panel includes league and referee-body representatives, so it is only partly independent.
course_use: Short discussion of auditing. Free.

title: How VAR and referee actually reach a decision on shared video
author_source: Mehmet Ali Icbay, WU Vienna, Journal of Sport and Social Issues, 2026, peer-reviewed article
note: Conversation analysis of 107 official VAR recordings from Turkey's 2024-25 season, with three episodes examined in depth. Shows the same video can be read differently because of professional vision and accountability, challenging the idea that video is objective. Author is at WU, so a possible guest speaker. Qualitative and one league.
course_use: Reading on video and interpretation; possible WU guest. Paid journal; check WU licence.

title: Bundesliga Match Facts: how xGoals is calculated
author_source: DFL / Bundesliga.com with Sportec Solutions and AWS, article
note: German-language explanation of a tracking-based xG model built on about 40,000 historical shots, using distance, angle, shooter speed, defenders in the line of shot and goalkeeper coverage. Shows what tracking data adds to a simple shot-location model. League and vendor source.
course_use: Background and lab motivation for xG. Free, in German.

title: Bundesliga Match Fact: Match Momentum
author_source: AWS for M&E Blog, September 2025, vendor technical post (developed by Sportec Solutions with DFL)
note: Unusually transparent recipe: nine offensive indicators in a sliding five-minute window, normalised and shown on a -10 to +10 scale, on 25 Hz positional and event feeds. Good for deconstructing a metric. Vendor claims about value are not independently tested.
course_use: Class exercise: rebuild or critique the metric. Free.

title: DFL Bundesliga Data Shootout on Kaggle
author_source: DFL, AWS, Sportec Solutions, Kaggle competition, 2022
note: Competition to detect plays, challenges and throw-ins in Bundesliga video, run from July to October 2022 with a 25,000 USD prize pool according to search results. Later winning SoccerNet teams drew on its top solutions. Task details were not visible on the fetched page; a Kaggle login is needed to read solution write-ups.
course_use: Computer vision lab or demonstration. Free with Kaggle account.

title: SoccerNet 2025 Challenges Results
author_source: Giancola, Cioppa and 116 others, arXiv preprint 2508.19182, 2025
note: Fifth edition of the benchmark: team ball action spotting, monocular depth estimation, multi-view foul recognition and game state reconstruction. Shows the state of the art for automatic tagging and for rebuilding a 2D pitch view from broadcast. Preprint, and only the abstract page was checked for this row.
course_use: Background for the computer vision part. Free.

title: FIFA Women's World Cup 2023 tournament analysis
author_source: FIFA Technical Study Group, FIFA Training Centre, 2023, tournament analysis site
note: Technical, tactical and physical findings from the women's tournament; search results describe a team of 52 analysts. A real example of governing-body analysis at a major women's event. Full contents were not read for this row.
course_use: Background; women's football comparison. Free.

title: Inside Bundesliga opposition analysis: Benjamin Glück at TSG Hoffenheim
author_source: Goal.com / SPOX, 2019, interview (German)
note: Hoffenheim's video analyst under Nagelsmann describes analysing three or four opposition matches by four phases, showing about twelve scenes, sending clips to phones, dropping drones, and starting opposition analysis only at U17. One of the most concrete German-language analyst accounts found; a single club and 2019 practice.
course_use: Reading and discussion. Free, in German.

title: Red Bull Academy Salzburg: match analysis and technology
author_source: The Red Bulletin, article, featuring head of match analysis Alexander Schmalhofer
note: Describes LPM tracking at 25 Hz, the SoccerBot360 training environment, packing scores and in-house AI video recognition said to save about 1.5 analyst working days. Schmalhofer stresses that data without context is useless and that players respond best to video. Austrian example, but owner-published and promotional. No account from RB Leipzig analysts was found.
course_use: Discussion or starting point for an invited guest. Free.

title: From Rapid Wien video analyst to Rangnick's right hand at the ÖFB
author_source: Salzburg24, March 2026, news profile (German)
note: Career of Stefan Oesen: Rapid Wien video analyst, FC Liefering, ÖFB match analyst, now head of science, analysis and development under Rangnick. Useful as an Austrian career path and guest-speaker lead. Says little about methods. No detailed interview with Salzburg, Sturm Graz or Rapid analysts was found.
course_use: Career discussion and guest-speaker lead. Free, in German.

title: Daniel Link: AI is only one piece in football
author_source: Technical University of Munich, July 2026, interview (German)
note: German sports informatics professor on skeletal data, scanning and fatigue estimation, the need to filter data, and the need to validate indicators. Notes that it can hardly be shown that AI decides wins, and that amateur two-camera systems have higher error rates. Timely and sober.
course_use: Short reading to open a discussion on AI. Free, in German.

title: A week in the job: Sam Green at LA Galaxy
author_source: StatsBomb Data Diaries, blog interview
note: Day-by-day account of an assistant coach and video lead: 8-10 minute annotated videos, 20-minute team meetings, Power BI dashboards on StatsBomb data, a set-piece dashboard, and a live iPad feed at the bench. Very concrete; published by a data vendor and describes one club.
course_use: Reading; students map the workflow. Free.

title: Brentford bring set-piece prowess to the Premier League
author_source: Training Ground Guru, October 2021, article
note: Set-piece work tied to sister club Midtjylland: xG per corner as the measure, a playbook covering every situation, and a full-time staff member designing variations for each opponent. Includes an opposing analyst's view. Early-season sample of seven matches.
course_use: Case illustration for the set-piece topic. Free archive.

title: FC Midtjylland and football's data revolution
author_source: Sean Ingle, The Guardian, October 2020, republished by Yahoo Sports
note: Rasmus Ankersen and head performance analyst Søren Bjerg on expected-goals recruitment, thousands of set pieces reviewed to build a playbook of 20-25 routines, and a captain's claim that 49% of goals came from set pieces. Good journalistic source; success claims are the club's own.
course_use: Reading for the mini-case on Midtjylland and Brentford. Free.

title: How Chelsea uses analytics on matchday
author_source: DataFramed podcast no. 114, DataCamp, November 2022, interview with Federico Bettuzzi
note: A club data scientist on event and 25 fps tracking data, a live mobile app showing cumulative xG, and an automated set-piece project. Claims a dramatic set-piece improvement without showing causal evidence, which makes a good class critique.
course_use: Listening task. Free.

title: FC Viktoria Berlin: a part-time analyst in women's football
author_source: Veo, article on its website
note: German 2. Frauen-Bundesliga club with a part-time analyst working remotely about 500 km away: opposition analysis due Monday evening, Tuesday review with the coach, and about 20-minute player sessions with handouts. Practical low-resource example, but vendor-published and unverified.
course_use: Discussion of women's and low-budget analysis. Free.

title: zone14: AI video analysis for Austrian amateur clubs
author_source: Trending Topics, September 2021, news article (German)
note: Vienna start-up with a self-installed 4K camera and cloud platform for amateur clubs, with partners including Wiener Sportclub and FK Austria Wien. Local counterpart to Veo and Trace. Article dates from 2021, current status was not checked.
course_use: Local market example. Free, in German.

title: Trace report on video in youth soccer
author_source: Trace, April 2023, company press release
note: Company survey of 100 US club directors, useful only as an example of how grassroots video is marketed. Vendor data. No independent evaluation of Veo or Trace was found. The page blocked automated fetching, so it is known from search results only.
course_use: Critical reading of vendor claims. Free.

title: Test your code windows and agree deadlines before matchday
author_source: World Rugby Passport, performance analysis course, governing-body guidance
note: Advises designing and testing code and output windows and capture equipment in advance, agreeing when coding is due, and limiting live capture to what supports coaches' decisions. Rugby guidance, included because no comparable public football federation guide was found; it transfers but is not football evidence.
course_use: Practical checklist for a lab. Free.

fields.practice: Design and test your code window and capture kit before matchday, and keep live coding to what supports the coach's in-game decisions.

title: Treat live codes as provisional
author_source: Bruce, Dwyer, Fox, PLoS ONE, 2022, peer-reviewed article
note: Two coders coded eight netball matches live, then twice from video. Video coding was more reliable, and live coding undercounted events, especially high-frequency ones. Netball and only two coders, so transfer to football is an inference.
course_use: Reading and reliability lab design. Open access.

fields.practice: Re-code important events from video after the match instead of relying on live counts.

title: Plan the week backwards from matchday
author_source: StatsBomb Data Diaries, interview with Sam Green, LA Galaxy, blog
note: One club's cycle: review the last match and build team video on MD-4, finalise and present on MD-3, set pieces and direct-opponent clips on MD-2, short meeting and live feed on matchday. A single-club account; no study compares weekly cycles.
course_use: Students draft a weekly plan. Free.

fields.practice: Fix the outputs and meetings for each day counting back from matchday.

title: Delay the main video review
author_source: Wright, Carling and others, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2016, peer-reviewed article
note: 48 players from three English Championship clubs completed a questionnaire and 22 were interviewed. Most preferred 24 to 48 hours between match and video feedback. Preference data and one country and level, with no measure of learning.
course_use: Reading on feedback timing. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Schedule the main player review 24 to 48 hours after the match unless the fixture list forces earlier delivery.

title: Separate the quick debrief from the deep review
author_source: Nicholls, James and others, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2018, peer-reviewed article
note: Structured interviews with 23 analysts in Olympic sports. Feedback tended to be either under 10 minutes within an hour of performance, or 25 minutes or more the next day, usually coach-led for video. Describes habit, not effectiveness, and is not football.
course_use: Discussion of feedback formats. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Keep any immediate debrief under ten minutes and save the detailed session for the next day.

title: Validate the coding tool with experts first
author_source: Torreblanca-Martínez et al., Cuadernos de Psicología del Deporte, 2024, peer-reviewed article
note: Six-phase design of a tool for crosses, with five experts and two observers; 125 crosses were coded and kappa averaged above 0.86. A model process for building a code window. The tool has 285 categories, far too many for matchday use.
course_use: Template for a student coding project. Open journal, in Spanish with English abstract.

fields.practice: Define categories with expert review and a pilot before using a code window at scale.

title: Weigh detail against reliability
author_source: Peter O'Donoghue, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2007, peer-reviewed article
note: Conceptual paper with 120 citations: clear definitions do not guarantee reliability, some statistics look acceptable even for different matches, and more precise measures trade off reliability. Argues reliability matters as much in coaching as in research.
course_use: Core reading on reliability. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Add a tag only if the extra detail justifies the loss of reliability it brings.

title: Run an inter-operator check with kappa
author_source: Liu, Hopkins and others, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2013, peer-reviewed article
note: Two groups of trained operators independently coded one La Liga match in the Opta system; kappa was 0.92 and 0.94 and event timing differed by 0.06 s. A template for a check, but one match and professional operators, so club-level coders should expect lower values. Bradley et al. 2007 report a similar test for ProZone.
course_use: Basis for a two-coder class lab. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Have two trained people code the same match independently and compute kappa per event type before trusting the data.

title: Report detection and classification agreement together
author_source: Rafnsson, O'Donoghue and others, Behavioral Sciences, 2026, peer-reviewed pilot
note: A single expert re-coded youth defenders from 16 matches. Kappa among matched events was 0.917, but event-detection agreement was 73.3% and combined kappa fell to 0.427. Shows how kappa on matched events alone flatters a tool. Pilot, single observer.
course_use: Excellent reliability teaching example. Open access.

fields.practice: Count missed and extra events in your reliability figure and do not report agreement only on events both coders found.

title: Do not treat one reading of video as objective
author_source: Furley, Mehta, Raabe, Memmert, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2025, peer-reviewed article
note: Three studies, 55 coaches: asked basic questions on an opponent, including formation, coaches agreed poorly, with Fleiss kappa from slightly below zero to fair. Strong caution for opposition analysis. Small samples and tasks that differ from a staff discussion.
course_use: Replicate in class: students watch a clip and answer independently. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.area: inter- and intra-rater reliability; opposition reports
fields.practice: Have at least two people judge the opponent independently and compare before writing conclusions.

title: Choose KPIs with the coach
author_source: Wright, Atkins, Jones, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2012, peer-reviewed article
note: Survey of 46 elite and semi-professional coaches: 91% said coaching philosophy shapes KPI choice and 43% cited gut instinct. Multiple sports and self-report. Describes how KPIs are selected, not whether those KPIs are valid.
course_use: Reading and KPI workshop. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Derive the KPI set from the coach's game model and write down why each one is included.

title: Do not judge teams by possession share
author_source: Wang, Qin and others, PLoS ONE, 2022, systematic review
note: Review of 75 studies from 2000 to 2020 concluded that match outcome is not related to possession percentage and that definitions differ across studies. Supports process and style indicators over a single aggregate.
course_use: Reading on KPI validity. Open access.

fields.practice: Replace possession percentage with indicators of where and how the ball is won, moved and lost.

title: Show few scenes
author_source: Benjamin Glück, TSG Hoffenheim, interview, Goal.com / SPOX, 2019
note: Hoffenheim's analyst says the team sees about twelve scenes picked with the coaches from a larger pool, and that overloaded players retain little. One club's practice under one coach; the number has not been tested.
course_use: Discussion with the recall evidence below. Free, in German.

fields.practice: Select about a dozen scenes with the coaching staff and leave the rest out of the team meeting.

title: Limit messages: players forget most feedback
author_source: Mason, Farrow, Hattie, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2020, peer-reviewed article
note: Six coach-player pairs at an AFL club: coaches gave nearly 30 feedback messages per one-to-one video meeting; players recalled 50% of summarised messages but 6% of all feedback a week later. Very small sample and Australian rules football, but it is one of the few studies measuring recall.
course_use: Key reading for feedback design. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Cut each player meeting to a few messages and test what the player can recall later.

title: Cut clips to 30 to 60 seconds
author_source: Veo, how-to article, vendor guidance
note: Recommends 30 to 60 second clips of plays, set pieces and defensive sequences, with annotation. Vendor advice without evidence. No research on optimal clip length in football was found, so treat this as a starting convention; LA Galaxy's edited videos run 8-10 minutes in total.
course_use: Clip-editing lab rule of thumb. Free.

fields.practice: Keep each clip to about 30 to 60 seconds, showing the build-up only if the teaching point needs it.

title: Balance positive and corrective clips
author_source: Groom, Cushion, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2005, peer-reviewed article
note: Case study of 10 professional youth players: video sessions increased understanding, but some players found negative examples harder and confidence could suffer. Old and small, with no ratio tested. No experiment establishing an ideal ratio of positive to corrective clips was found.
course_use: Reading on the psychology of feedback. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Include positive examples in every session and check privately how individual players react to criticism.

title: Ask before you tell
author_source: Raya-Castellano, Reeves and others, International Journal of Performance Analysis in Sport, 2020, peer-reviewed article
note: 22 team video sessions by four junior-elite coaches: delivery was prescriptive, dominated by feedback, with some silence and player participation and a gap between what coaches understood and what they did. A follow-up 23-month development programme (Raya-Castellano et al., 2021) raised coaches' understanding of questioning. Small, and player learning was not measured.
course_use: Students code a filmed feedback session. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Pause each teaching clip and ask players what they see before giving your reading.

title: Match group or individual delivery to the message
author_source: Middlemas, Harwood, Journal of Applied Sport Psychology, 2018, peer-reviewed interview study
note: Interviews with 11 coaches and 12 players in elite youth football on psychological responses, delivery strategies and climate in video sessions. Read at abstract level: the choice between individual and group delivery is the applied inference. Wright et al. (2016) also found that interaction levels varied widely between sessions.
course_use: Reading on delivery climate. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Decide per message whether it belongs in the group or in a private session, considering how exposed a player will feel.

title: Agree expectations and hierarchy early
author_source: Bateman, Jones, Frontiers in Psychology, 2019, peer-reviewed interview study
note: Six elite football analysts: open and honest relationships were rated highest, conflict arose mainly from unmet coach expectations, and the relationship is largely dictated by the coach. Analyst-only view and a small sample.
course_use: Reading and role play. Open access.

fields.practice: Agree in writing at the start what the coach expects, by when and in what format.

title: Decide openly how to handle information you might withhold
author_source: Nelson, James, and others, Sport, Education and Society, 2023, peer-reviewed article
note: Survey of 88 analysts across sports: trustworthiness was central to work relationships and careers, and analysts often concealed information, with coaches, to spare players or when data did not fit the coach's approach. Booroff et al. (2016) similarly show a coach using video politically. Self-report and mixed sports.
course_use: Ethics discussion. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Agree with the coach when information is withheld from players and why, and do not misrepresent data.

title: Structure opposition analysis by phases
author_source: Benjamin Glück, TSG Hoffenheim, interview, Goal.com / SPOX, 2019
note: Analyses three or four matches of the opponent, depending on formations used, across possession, opposition possession and both transitions, to identify spaces and ball-winning moments. Single practitioner; widely used structure but not tested. Read with Furley et al. on coach disagreement.
course_use: Template for a student opposition report. Free, in German.

fields.practice: Base the report on three or four relevant matches, sorted by the four phases of play and ending in concrete plans.

title: Code corners with a standard set of variables
author_source: Plakias, Armatas, Giakas, Applied Sciences, 2025, systematic review
note: 21 studies on male soccer. Dynamic attacks with 3-4 players and indirect far-post deliveries were linked to more shots on target; mixed marking with near-post cover to fewer goals conceded. Zone definitions were inconsistent and only two studies covered the transition after losing the ball. A related meta-analysis by the same team puts goal conversion at about 3%, so judge routines by shots and first contact.
course_use: Basis for a corner coding lab. Open access.

fields.practice: Record delivery, number of attackers, movement, marking and the transition after the corner, and judge routines by shots as well as goals.

title: Analyse throw-ins too
author_source: Stone, Smith, Barry, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2021, peer-reviewed article
note: 16,154 throw-ins in 380 Premier League matches in 2018-19. Backward and lateral throws improved first contact, retention and shot creation; long forward throws were least efficient. One league and observational, with style confounds likely.
course_use: Data exercise. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Include throw-ins in set-piece analysis and track first contact and retention by direction.

title: Adapt analysis to the academy phase
author_source: Dhillon, Nicholls, Woodward, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2025, peer-reviewed article
note: Survey of 65 English academy coaches: PA use grew strongly from foundation to professional development phase, shaped by time, resources and buy-in, and EPPP guidance on distribution was insufficient. English system; self-report. Hoffenheim's analyst likewise reported starting opposition work only at U17.
course_use: Discussion of academy provision. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Plan what analysis each age phase receives, with younger groups focused on individual learning and not opposition detail.

title: Do not copy men's benchmarks into women's football
author_source: Harkness-Armstrong, Till and others, PLoS ONE, 2022, systematic review
note: 69 studies: physical data dominate (47) and only two reported tactical characteristics; velocity and acceleration thresholds are inconsistent. Maneiro et al. (2019) also report different corner models in the men's and women's World Cups. Evidence gaps remain large.
course_use: Reading for the women's football part. Open access.

fields.practice: Use women's-specific references and state the thresholds you apply when comparing data.

title: Plan around scarce resources in women's football
author_source: Harkness-Armstrong, Seth and others, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2024, peer-reviewed survey
note: 39 practitioners surveyed in 2023 at international to youth level: team (100%), opposition (84%) and individual (79%) analysis were common; 31 named challenges including limited resources (42%), data availability and facilities. Small convenience sample.
course_use: Discussion and possible survey replication in Austria. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Before designing a workflow, audit which footage, data and staff time are actually available at that level.

title: Film from a high halfway-line position
author_source: Veo, how-to article, vendor guidance; also Hudl, how to record a football match
note: Touchline at halfway, as high as possible, 3 to 5 metres on a full-size pitch, camera straight across and left alone once recording. Hudl also advises testing at a friendly and carrying spare power and storage. Vendor sources that sell cameras, but the basic geometry is consistent across guides; no independent test was found.
course_use: Practical guidance for student filming. Free.

fields.practice: Fix an elevated camera at the halfway line so both penalty areas are visible, and test it at a friendly first.

title: Use video as a conversation at amateur level
author_source: Fele, Campagnolo, Sports Coaching Review, 2023, peer-reviewed article
note: Multimodal analysis of tactical video sessions at an amateur club shows players labelling stills, re-enacting and zooming out, with the coach as only one voice. Single case. Nyman et al. (2025) warn of workload and insufficient resources for manual video work.
course_use: Reading on video as social practice. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Run short discussion-based sessions on a few moments rather than attempting full professional coding.

title: Store data with a purpose and a deletion date
author_source: World Rugby Passport, data storage and protection page, governing-body guidance
note: Collect only with a clear purpose, keep only as long as needed, set a review and deletion point, and store personal data securely. High-level and rugby-based, with nothing on backups. Football-specific guidance on file management is thin and mostly from storage vendors.
course_use: Starter policy exercise. Free.

fields.practice: Define for each dataset why it is kept and when it is reviewed or deleted.

title: Check the tracking provider's FIFA test report
author_source: FIFA Quality Programme for EPTS, governing-body standard
note: FIFA Basic covers safety; FIFA Quality adds performance tests for positioning and velocity. Tested providers have publicly available reports showing accuracy by velocity bracket. Accuracy for position and speed does not validate derived tactical metrics.
course_use: Exercise: compare two providers' reports. Free.

fields.practice: Read the published accuracy report for the speeds that matter before buying or trusting tracking data.

title: Have a processor contract and breach procedure
author_source: The FA with Muckle LLP, UK GDPR Guide, 2021, governing-body guidance
note: Clubs need to know whether they are controller or processor, keep a clear retention policy, and report relevant breaches within 72 hours. Written for English grassroots clubs and under UK GDPR, so Austrian DSB and DSGVO requirements need checking. Says nothing specific about video analysis.
course_use: Legal checklist. Free PDF.

fields.practice: Identify your role for each data flow, sign processor agreements with video vendors, and prepare a 72-hour breach procedure.

title: Apply extra protection to under-16 players
author_source: The FA with Muckle LLP, UK GDPR Guide, 2021, governing-body guidance
note: Asks clubs to write privacy notices in plain language for under-16s and notes parental consent may be needed for online services. UK rule of thumb, and the digital-consent age differs across EU states, including Austria, so verify locally before using this for youth footage. Not specific to video.
course_use: Discussion on youth footage and uploads. Free PDF.

fields.practice: Give young players and parents a plain-language notice on filming and uploading, and obtain parental consent where required.

title: Treat performance data as personal data
author_source: C. Flanagan, Entertainment and Sports Law Journal, 2021, peer-reviewed article
note: Reviews the legal issues of football data, in light of the reported Project Red Card action on systematic use of player data. Legal commentary on a claim that remained unresolved in the sources seen. Overkamp (2025) covers portability under Art. 20 DSGVO for a German-language reader.
course_use: Reading for data ethics; a legal guest may help. Open journal.

fields.practice: Treat tagged and tracked player data as personal data with a stated legal basis and defined sharing.

title: Build relational as well as technical skills
author_source: Nicholls, Groom and others, International Journal of Sports Science and Coaching, 2026, peer-reviewed interview study
note: 38 UK analysts with about seven years' experience: effective practice combines technical skills in data, video and analysis with trust, credibility, adaptability and communication. McKenna et al. (2018), with six interns, similarly found that relationships had to be built first. UK elite focus and self-report.
course_use: Competency framework for course design. Paid journal; check WU licence.

fields.practice: Develop communication, trust-building and tactical knowledge alongside tagging tools and data skills.

title: Add data skills and a shared metric glossary
author_source: Lolli, Bauer and others, Science and Medicine in Football, 2024, peer-reviewed survey
note: 29 national federations and 32 clubs: applied data analytics expertise was underemployed, governance perceptions varied, and metric taxonomies were missing; only about 30% of federation respondents found positional data from providers sufficiently clear. Self-report from a self-selected practitioner community.
course_use: Discussion on hiring and coding skills. Paid journal; check WU licence.
